blocks.text: Filter Methods, Correlation, Chi-Square, and ANOVA together completed this module first family, fast, statistical, and entirely independent of any actual model. Wrapper methods open a genuinely different philosophy entirely, actually training a real model repeatedly with different candidate feature subsets, and using genuine, real performance to decide which features actually earn their place.

This topic covers how wrapper methods genuinely work, wrapping an actual model training process inside a search loop, the real, genuine advantage this approach has over filter methods, capturing feature interactions and reflecting a specific model actual behavior, the real, often severe computational cost this accuracy demands, a genuine overfitting risk the search process itself can introduce, and a preview of the three specific search strategies the rest of this module family covers.
1. How Wrapper Methods Actually Work

blocks.alt: A feature subset trains a model, then its performance gets checked

blocks.text: A wrapper method genuinely takes a candidate subset of features, trains an actual, real model using only those features, and measures that model genuine, real performance directly, accuracy, error, whatever metric actually matters for the problem. This process repeats across genuinely many different candidate subsets, with the subset producing the genuinely best real performance ultimately selected.

This is genuinely, fundamentally different from every filter method technique covered so far, there is no generic statistical score computed in isolation, the actual, real model itself is the judge of which features genuinely matter, wrapped directly inside the selection process, exactly where this family name comes from.
2. The Real Advantage: Capturing Feature Interactions

blocks.alt: Wrapper methods genuinely see real feature interactions

blocks.text: Because an actual model genuinely considers the entire feature subset together during training, wrapper methods genuinely capture interaction effects that filter methods structurally cannot see, exactly the real limitation flagged back in Filter Methods. Two features that each look genuinely weak on their own by a filter method score might combine to produce a genuinely strong real signal, something only an actual trained model evaluating them together can detect.

This is genuinely the core reason wrapper methods exist at all, despite their real computational cost, when genuine feature interactions matter for a specific problem, no amount of independent, per feature scoring can substitute for actually training a real model and watching how it performs.
3. A Genuinely Model Specific Advantage

blocks.alt: Wrapper methods get tuned to one specific model

blocks.text: Because wrapper methods genuinely train the actual model intended for real deployment, the resulting feature subset is optimized specifically for that model real, particular behavior, not a generic, model agnostic statistical score that might not translate well to how that specific algorithm actually learns. A feature set genuinely optimized for a tree based model might genuinely differ from one optimized for a linear model, and wrapper methods genuinely capture that real difference directly.

This model specificity is a genuine, real strength, but it also means a wrapper method feature selection genuinely does not transfer automatically to a different model the way a filter method selection generally does, worth keeping in mind when comparing these two families directly.

blocks.text: 4. The Real, Often Severe Computational Cost

blocks.alt: Many subsets to try means retraining the model each time

blocks.text: Every candidate feature subset genuinely requires training an entire, separate model from scratch, and the genuine number of possible subsets grows explosively with the number of features, a dataset with just 20 features already has over a million possible subsets to consider in principle. This real, often severe computational cost is exactly why filter methods, covered in the previous four topics, are almost always worth running first.

In practice, wrapper methods genuinely never try every possible subset exhaustively, instead relying on the smarter, more efficient search strategies previewed later in this topic and covered in the specific topics that follow, forward selection, backward elimination, and recursive feature elimination.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Wrapper methods real computational cost grows explosively with feature count. This is exactly why running filter methods first, to narrow down the candidate features, is genuinely worth doing before ever reaching for a wrapper method.

blocks.text: 5. A Worked Example
A minimal wrapper method, evaluating two candidate feature subsets directly against real model performance, shows the core mechanism in its simplest possible form.

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
import pandas as pd

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "square_feet": [900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100, 2400],
    "bedrooms": [2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5],
    "shoe_size_unrelated": [8, 9, 7, 10, 8, 9],
})
y = pd.Series([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1])

score_all = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X, y, cv=3).mean()
score_relevant = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X[["square_feet", "bedrooms"]], y, cv=3).mean()

print("All features:", score_all)
print("Relevant subset only:", score_relevant)

blocks.text: This is genuinely the entire wrapper method idea, at its smallest possible scale, two candidate subsets, two real models actually trained and evaluated, with the genuinely better performing subset winning out, exactly the mechanism the rest of this module family scales up into real, systematic search strategies.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Always run filter methods first to narrow down an initial candidate feature list before ever applying a wrapper method. This genuinely keeps the wrapper method search space small enough to be computationally practical.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuine Overfitting Risk in the Search Itself

blocks.alt: Searching over many subsets can overfit to the validation set

blocks.text: Trying many candidate subsets and picking whichever performs genuinely best on a single validation split carries a real, subtle risk, with enough subsets tried, one might simply look good by pure chance on that one specific split, without genuinely reflecting a real, generalizable pattern at all, essentially the same overfitting concept covered back in Polynomial Features, now applied to the search process itself rather than a single model.

The genuine, standard fix is evaluating every candidate subset using cross validation rather than a single train test split, exactly the technique briefly used in the worked example above, and covered in full, rigorous depth in the dedicated Cross Validation module later in this course.
7. Three Genuine Search Strategies Ahead

blocks.alt: Wrapper methods include forward selection, backward elimination, and recursive feature elimination

blocks.text: Since trying every possible subset exhaustively is genuinely impractical, as covered above, this module remaining wrapper method topics each cover a genuine, smarter search strategy instead. Forward selection genuinely starts from zero features and adds one at a time. Backward elimination genuinely starts from every feature and removes one at a time. Recursive feature elimination refines that backward approach into a genuinely more systematic, model informed process.
Each of these three genuine strategies makes a different, real tradeoff between search thoroughness and computational cost, covered directly, one at a time, in the three topics that follow this one.
